newsitem.title: GERMANY: German trade competitiveness rising - institutes. [CORRECTED 11:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: German trade competitiveness rising - institutes. [CORRECTED 11:25 GMT]

text.p: Germany's six leading economic think-tanks said on Tuesday that moderate wage demands and measures to reduce labour costs in the past year had led to a rise in Germany's international competitiveness.
The institutes said in their spring report that west German unit labour costs measured in deutschemarks would fall around 1.5 percent over 1996 and 1997 together.

Over the same time-period, unit labour costs in the United States and the rest of Europe would rise six percent and three percent respectively, they estimated. (Corrects to show six percent figure refers to United States, not rest of Europe.)

The institutes nonetheless added that the German labour market, with unemployment remaining stubbornly at record highs, was still "under extreme tension" and that east German wage levels had a long way to go before they returned to what they considered "normal" levels.

German firms had however benefitted from the reduction in labour costs by posting profits that were "significantly improved", a result of their not fully passing on the benefits of lower labour costs to consumers, the institutes said.
The think-tanks' report also included an optimistic analysis of the potential impact of European monetary union (EMU) on the continent's labour market.

While it acknowledged the argument that EMU reduced the ability of governments to smooth out regional labour market difficulties with monetary policy, it said differences in wage conditions across Europe need not be a problem.

"International trade is always about give and take. Those countries at the bottom of the wage hierachy can profit with products that involve a low degree of capital. They in turn purchase capital-intensive products from countries at the top end (in terms of wages).
